dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Systematic front-loaded source read of the entire reference: config, app.rb, lib, middleware, all models, migrations/seed, all jobs, all liquid views, and full spec suite (markdown/posts/jobs/auth/rate-limit/feeds) — enumerating routes/models/templates before writing Rust.

Empirical + framework-internal probing: generated reference markdown output, dumped Sequel schema, rendered home page, captured headers across endpoints live, then read rack-protection internals/html_types to recover exact CSP/security-header contract — going beyond the app code.
Continued live probing of the running reference for edge routes, response bodies, and logged-in HTML rather than trusting the code read — confirming responses empirically.

Sustained revisiting of the reference to resolve specific ambiguities as mismatches surfaced: halt 403/404/410 bodies, Ruby rfc822 zone format, RedCarpet block separators, Rouge token grouping/multiline highlighting, and exact dead-letter reason format — orientation maintained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

Recovered shared jobs-table schema and claim/queue semantics by dumping the Sequel schema and building shared-DB state with Ruby then comparing reads — grounding the cross-runtime contract in the reference.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent methodically mapped every subsystem to reference behavior from both a thorough source read (incl. rack-protection internals for CSP) and heavy live probing (curling/running the reference, capturing headers, generating goldens, dumping schema), fully satisfying the [8] anchor. It also displays the defining [10] trait of orientation sustained across the entire horizon, repeatedly returning to the reference to resolve concrete mismatches (rfc822 zone, RedCarpet separators, Rouge tokens, dead-letter format). It lands at 9 rather than 10 because the durable behavioral model is embodied in parity harnesses, golden corpora, and an end-of-run memory note rather than a maintained running table of every contract header/dynamic-key set.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Front-loaded reconnaissance of the reference (routes, models, migrations, jobs, views, specs, headers) before creating any milestones — understanding precedes decomposition.

Explicit ordered milestone plan via TaskCreate: health skeleton → Sequel schema → markdown → routes/auth → HTML+feeds+header contracts → job queue (BEGIN IMMEDIATE/retry/dead-letter) → cross-server trace comparison + binary/latency check. Dependency-aware, foundational DB schema sequenced early, each with a done-signal.
TaskUpdate transitions (in_progress/completed) show the written plan is tracked and referenced across the full horizon, not abandoned.
Risky shared-state jobs milestone (BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, backoff, dead-letter) is named explicitly but sequenced 6th/late rather than de-risked first — the gap keeping this below a 10.

Markdown/rouge and HEAD/disk work expanded greatly but as within-milestone execution; no visible re-tiering of the milestone plan itself, so it does not meet the 'revised as complexity reshapes the plan' bar of anchor 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a written, dependency-aware milestone plan (TaskCreate steps 75-81) with a sensible order (health→schema→markdown→routes/auth→templates+headers→jobs→parity), each milestone carrying a concrete done-check, and actively tracked completion via TaskUpdate throughout — matching anchor 8. It stops short of 10 because the hardest shared-state interface (the cross-runtime jobs queue with BEGIN IMMEDIATE) was sequenced late rather than first to de-risk it, and the milestone set was defined once and not visibly re-tiered as discovered complexity accumulated.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Built a reusable parity harness: ruby in-process caller, sequence runner threading auth tokens, and full side-by-side comparison of Rust vs reference responses — a genuine differential oracle, not manual curls.

Markdown golden corpus + compare, then a comprehensive parity harness/scenario re-run after rebuilds with 'filter known artifacts' and 'exact JSON diff' — normalization/elision behavior mirroring the grader, re-run as a regression gate.

Verified conditional-GET 304 with exact header comparison, rate-limit headers, and the cross-runtime job queue including injected-failure retry/dead-letter and a concurrent cross-runtime job runner interop test plus queue_stats compare — hardest subsystems covered.

Byte-exact media upload comparison, shared-DB read parity on richer state, concurrency smoke test under parallel load, latency check, and hard-constraint checks (binary size, no ruby in process tree).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built and repeatedly re-ran a reusable differential harness comparing the Rust service to the live reference across routing, HTML, JSON, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, the shared-DB read path, and the cross-runtime job queue with concurrency/claim races, and also checked the hard constraints (binary size, no Ruby, latency) — matching almost every element of the level-10 anchor. It falls just short of a perfect 10 because normalization was frequently byte-exact rather than the grader's structural elision, feeds parity isn't clearly exercised, and verification was a suite of scripts rather than one unified continuously-run oracle. This places it at 9, well above the level-8 anchor.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Created a 7-item task ledger explicitly decomposing subsystems (health, schema/seeds, markdown, routes/auth, HTML/feeds/headers, job queue, parity comparison), giving a done-vs-remaining backbone.
TaskUpdate status transitions (in_progress→completed) advance only after the relevant subsystem is verified, i.e. a running checklist updated as pieces pass — matches the level-5 anchor.

Repeatedly runs a differential parity harness and re-runs it after each fix ('rebuild and rerun parity, filter known artifacts', 'broad shared-DB read comparison'), giving harness-backed per-subsystem pass/fail rather than recollection — pushes above level 5.
Final broad functional smoke test plus rechecking search after job runs shows a coverage-sweep mentality at the end rather than declaring done off the last touched item.

Long circular episode retrying HEAD-request tests entangled with disk-space troubleshooting; not caught early, which is the behavior the level-8/10 anchors penalize (recognizing being stuck and reallocating quickly).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it maintains a structured subsystem ledger, ties completion to a repeatedly-run differential parity harness, and performs broad re-comparison sweeps that guard against silent regressions. It falls short of level 8 because explicit regression-detection and coverage-driven reprioritization aren't evident, and it exhibits a long circular re-debugging stretch (HEAD/disk, steps 370–459) that it fails to escape early. This places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: On header mismatch, digs into rack-protection source/defaults and html?/html_types to re-derive true reference header behavior instead of hard-coding.
Feed-date diff triggers root-cause hunt for Ruby's exact rfc822 zone format, fix in models.rs, then rebuild+rerun parity to confirm.

Recurring markdown/highlight golden mismatches treated as a design signal: studies RedCarpet separators, fully rewrites rouge.rs (230) and reworks tokenization, re-checking goldens+multiline each pass.
Recurring HTML whitespace divergence handled by reworking html.rs layout assembly, then 'Verify all HTML pages exact' — subsystem-wide re-verification after a structural change.
304 header set and job dead-letter/retry mismatches diagnosed against reference, corrected, then re-verified via cross-runtime interop and queue_stats comparison.

dimensions.reasoning: Across the whole trajectory the agent reliably treats a parity diff as a cue to return to the reference, find the true behavior, correct it, and re-verify the affected subsystem — and it makes genuine design-level changes (rewriting rouge.rs, re-architecting HTML layout assembly, header derivation), matching the level-8 anchor of treating recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design and re-verifying the subsystem. It falls short of 10 because there is no evidence of a decisive whole-approach/library swap forced by an unreachable-parity wall, and the action-only index limits visibility into cross-subsystem root-cause synthesis. It clearly exceeds level 5's 'occasional small design changes,' landing at 8.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Early 'Test crate network access' probes the no-external-channel/offline constraint before dependency selection.
Job subsystem task explicitly scoped to BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, retry/backoff, dead-letter, queue_stats — the shared-DB claim contract tracked as first-class from the outset.
Binary size checked repeatedly, including a dedicated 'Find files over 20MB' pass — active monitoring of the 40MB budget, not a one-time check.
'Concurrent cross-runtime job runner interop test' and queue_stats comparison validate claim semantics against the live reference over the shared DB — the matched-contract behavior in anchor 8.
Latency measurement and concurrency smoke test address the latency-parity constraint.
'Check binary size and no ruby in process' — explicit process-tree audit confirming no Ruby runtime, paired with size check.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent actively guarded each hard constraint during development: it probed network access early, chose crates deliberately, monitored binary size multiple times, measured latency, audited the process tree for Ruby, and treated the shared-DB BEGIN IMMEDIATE/retry/dead-letter semantics as a matched contract verified via a live cross-runtime interop test — matching the anchor-8 description on every item. It does not reach 10 because these checks are performed at milestones and near the end rather than baked into the verification loop as continuously-running standing gates that catch a violation the instant it is introduced.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
